smt-2014-algebra-01.title: Rates
smt-2014-algebra-01.body:
Together they paint half the house in 10 hours. In the second scenario the remaining half is painted by Alice alone in $30-10=20$ hours, so Alice paints the whole house in 40 hours (rate $\frac1{40}$ per hour). Together the rate is $\frac1{20}$, so Bob's rate is $\frac1{20}-\frac1{40}=\frac1{40}$: he needs 40 hours.

**Answer: 40 hours**

smt-2014-algebra-01.title: Equations
smt-2014-algebra-01.body:
Let Alice and Bob take $a$ and $b$ hours alone: $\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac1{20}$. First half takes 10 hours together, the second half takes Alice $\frac a2=20$ hours, so $a=40$ and $\frac1b=\frac1{20}-\frac1{40}=\frac1{40}$, $b=40$.

**Answer: 40 hours**

smt-2014-algebra-02.title: Binomial theorem
smt-2014-algebra-02.body:
The coefficients $1,6,15,20,15,6,1$ are $\binom6k$, so $9^6+6\cdot9^5+15\cdot9^4+20\cdot9^3+15\cdot9^2+6\cdot9+1=(9+1)^6=10^6$. The given sum lacks the final term $1$, so it equals $10^6-1=999999$.

**Answer: 999999**

smt-2014-algebra-04.title: Sign analysis of the quadratic
smt-2014-algebra-04.body:
Negating all of $x_1,x_2,x_3$ keeps the equation, so we may take $a_1=1$ and double the count at the end. Dividing by $x_1>0$, we study $t^2+bt+c=0$ with $t=x_4$ and $b=x_2/x_1$, $c=x_3/x_1$ of prescribed signs.

- $b>0,c>0$: roots have positive product and negative sum, so both are negative: $x_4<0$ only ($a_4=0$). Possible (e.g. $t=-1$).
- $b>0,c<0$: roots of opposite signs, so $x_4$ can be positive or negative (e.g. roots $1,-2$): $a_4\in\{0,1\}$.
- $b<0,c>0$: both roots positive, so $a_4=1$ only (e.g. $t=1$).
- $b<0,c<0$: opposite signs again: $a_4\in\{0,1\}$ (e.g. roots $2,-1$).

This gives $1+2+1+2=6$ tuples with $a_1=1$ (each pair $(a_2,a_3)$ with its allowed $a_4$), so $2\cdot6=12$.

**Answer: 12**

smt-2014-algebra-05.title: Reduce to two families
smt-2014-algebra-05.body:
Putting $x=0$ gives $\sin b=0$, so $b=n\pi$, and only the parity of $n$ matters (replacing $b$ by $b+2\pi$ changes nothing). With $b=0$: $\sin(ax)=\sin(29x)$ for all integers $x$. With $b=\pi$: $-\sin(ax)=\sin(29x)$, i.e. $\sin(ax)=\sin(-29x)$.

For integers $x=1$ and $x=2$, equal sines $\sin a=\sin c$ and $\sin2a=\sin2c$ give $\cos a=\cos c$ (when $\sin a\ne0$), so $a\equiv c\pmod{2\pi}$. Hence the possible $a$ are $a\equiv29\pmod{2\pi}$ (with $b=0$) or $a\equiv-29\pmod{2\pi}$ (with $b=\pi$).

The smallest positive numbers in these classes: $29-8\pi\approx3.87$ (since $8\pi\approx25.13$) and $10\pi-29\approx2.42$ (since $10\pi\approx31.42$). So the smallest is $10\pi-29$.

**Answer: $10\pi-29$**

smt-2014-algebra-06.title: AM-GM
smt-2014-algebra-06.body:
Let $a=x-y$, $b=y-z$, so $x-z=a+b$ and $ab(a+b)=17$. Then $\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac{a+b}{ab}=\frac{(a+b)^2}{17}$, so the expression is $E=\frac{s^2}{17}+\frac1s$ where $s=a+b$. Since $17=ab\,s\le\frac{s^3}4$ we have $s\ge\sqrt[3]{68}$, with equality at $a=b$. The function $\frac{s^2}{17}+\frac1s$ has derivative $\frac{2s}{17}-\frac1{s^2}$, positive when $s^3>\frac{17}2$, which holds for $s\ge\sqrt[3]{68}$ (as $68>8.5$), so $E$ is increasing there and is minimal at $s=\sqrt[3]{68}$: $E=\frac{68^{2/3}}{17}+\frac1{68^{1/3}}=\frac{4\cdot 17}{17\cdot 68^{1/3}}+\frac{1}{68^{1/3}}=\frac5{\sqrt[3]{68}}$ (using $68^{2/3}=68/68^{1/3}$ and $68/17=4$).

**Answer: $\dfrac{5}{\sqrt[3]{68}}$**

smt-2014-algebra-07.title: Double root
smt-2014-algebra-07.body:
As $q$ decreases, the cubic changes from one real root to three real roots exactly when it acquires a double root. At the threshold $f(x)=x^3+x^2+qx+9=(x-a)(x-b)^2$ with a simple root $a$ and a double root $b$. Vieta: $a+2b=-1$ and $ab^2=-9$. Substituting $a=-1-2b$: $(-1-2b)b^2=-9$, i.e. $2b^3+b^2-9=0$, which factors as $(2b-3)(b^2+2b+3)=0$ with only the real root $b=\frac32$. Then $a=-4$ and $q=b^2+2ab=\frac94-12=-\frac{39}4$.

For $q>-\frac{39}4$ the discriminant is negative (one real root); at $q=-\frac{39}4$ there is a double root (two distinct real roots), and below it there are three real roots. So $p=-\frac{39}4$.

**Answer: $-\frac{39}4$**

smt-2014-algebra-07.title: Discriminant
smt-2014-algebra-07.body:
The discriminant of $x^3+x^2+qx+9$ is $\Delta=18\cdot q\cdot9-4\cdot9+q^2-4q^3-27\cdot81=-4q^3+q^2+162q-2223$. It factors as $-(4q+39)(q^2-10q+57)$, and $q^2-10q+57>0$ always. So $\Delta<0\iff q>-\frac{39}4$, exactly the range with a single real root.

**Answer: $-\frac{39}4$**

smt-2014-algebra-08.title: Degrees
smt-2014-algebra-08.body:
Let $d=\deg P$. The left side has degree $d^2$. If $\deg Q<48$, the right side has degree $\max(16d,48)$; since $d^2=48$ is impossible, $d^2=16d$ and $d=16$. Comparing leading coefficients $c^{17}=c^{16}$ gives $c=1$, so $P(x)=x^{16}+R(x)$ with $\deg R<16$.

Then $P(P(x))-P(x)^{16}=R(P(x))=x^{48}+Q(x)$. Since $\deg R(P(x))=16\deg R=48$, we get $\deg R=3$, with leading coefficient 1 (to match $x^{48}$): $R(y)=y^3+\rho_2y^2+\rho_1y+\rho_0$. So $P(x)=x^{16}+x^3+O(x^2)$ and
$$Q(x)=R(P(x))-x^{48}=P^3+\rho_2P^2+\rho_1P+\rho_0-x^{48}.$$
Here $P^3=x^{48}+3x^{35}+O(x^{34})$, while $\rho_2P^2+\rho_1P+\rho_0$ has degree at most $32$. Therefore $Q=3x^{35}+O(x^{34})$ has degree exactly $35$ for every valid $P$, and $P=x^{16}+x^3$ is valid ($Q=3x^{35}+3x^{22}+x^9$).

**Answer: 35**

smt-2014-algebra-09.title: Telescoping bound
smt-2014-algebra-09.body:
Since $(k+2)^3+1=(k+3)(k^2+3k+3)=(k+3)a_k$, we have $k+2=\sqrt[3]{-1+a_k(k+3)}$. Let $r_k$ be the nested expression from level $k$ to $n$ (so $r_n=\sqrt[3]{-1+a_n}$, $r_k=\sqrt[3]{-1+a_kr_{k+1}}$, and $b_n=r_1$), and $s_k=k+2$, which satisfies $s_k=\sqrt[3]{-1+a_ks_{k+1}}$. Since $r_{n}<s_n$, induction gives $r_k<s_k$ for all $k$, so $b_n<s_1=3$.

For the gap $g_k=s_k-r_k$: $g_k=\frac{a_k(s_{k+1}-r_{k+1})}{s_k^2+s_kr_k+r_k^2}$, and $r_k\ge1$ (all $a_k\ge7$), so the denominator exceeds $s_k^2+s_k+1=(k+2)^2+(k+2)+1=a_{k+1}$. Thus $g_k<\frac{a_k}{a_{k+1}}g_{k+1}$, and so $g_1<\frac{a_1}{a_n}g_n<\frac{7(n+2)}{n^2+3n+3}\to0$. Hence $b_n=3-g_1\to3$ from below, and the smallest $L$ with $b_n<L$ for all $n$ is $L=3$.

**Answer: 3**

smt-2014-algebra-10.title: Telescoping
smt-2014-algebra-10.body:
Let $N=2014$ and $z_i=\frac{x_iy_N-y_ix_N}{y_N}=x_i+ay_i$ with $a=-\frac{x_N}{y_N}$. The sequence $z_i$ satisfies the same recurrence $z_{i}=-3z_{i-1}+z_{i-2}$, with $z_0=1$, $z_1=a$, $z_N=0$. We want $S=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}z_i^2$.

From the recurrence $z_{i-1}=z_{i+1}+3z_i$, so multiplying by $z_i$: $z_{i-1}z_i=z_iz_{i+1}+3z_i^2$. Hence $3z_i^2=w_{i-1}-w_i$ where $w_i=z_iz_{i+1}$. Summing for $i=1,\dots,N-1$ telescopes: $3\sum_{i=1}^{N-1}z_i^2=w_0-w_{N-1}=z_0z_1-z_{N-1}z_N=a$. Therefore $S=1+\frac a3=\frac{3y_N-x_N}{3y_N}$.

Since $x_i=y_{i-1}$ for all $i\ge1$ (both sides start $x_1=y_0=0$, $x_2=y_1=1$ and obey the same recurrence), $3y_N-x_N=3y_N-y_{N-1}=-y_{N+1}$, giving $S=-\frac{y_{2015}}{3y_{2014}}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3y_{2014}-x_{2014}}{3y_{2014}}=-\dfrac{y_{2015}}{3y_{2014}}$**
